title: How Eyewitness Testimony Works(?)
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss eyewitness testimony and why it is unreliable in criminal cases. They cover the 1959 Redmount brief on memory reliability, early psychologist Hugo Munsterberg and his book On the Witness Stand, later work by Robert Buckhout and Elizabeth Loftus, and the role of DNA exonerations and the Innocence Project. The hosts explain how perception and memory fill in gaps, the hollow-mask illusion, attentional blink, the psychological refractory period and weapon focus, and the cross-race effect. They describe how repeated recall, leading questions and misinformation effect build confidence, the Ronald Cotton and Bobby Poole case, the 1977 Supreme Court factors for eyewitness identification, and the Troy Davis execution. The episode closes with a listener mail about a dog named Scully and a family's road trip.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug upcoming live tour dates, then introduce the episode with a joke about a hit-and-run story and a friend's lineup experience.

segments.title: Eyewitness testimony as the courtroom gold standard
segments.summary: The hosts say eyewitness testimony is treated as the gold standard in courts and that juries find confident witnesses convincing, even when witnesses are wrong and sincere. They note DNA evidence has exposed many wrongful convictions and cite a 1959 brief by attorney Robert Redmount that presumed ordinary memory is reliable.

segments.title: Early psychology and Munsterberg's memory warnings
segments.summary: The hosts describe how early twentieth-century psychology examined memory reliability. Hugo Munsterberg wrote On the Witness Stand, showing through experiments at Harvard that memory is not a recording. His work was overlooked partly because of his pro-German statements during World War One.

segments.title: Smartphones, distraction and 1970s memory research
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how distraction, including smartphones, hurts witnesses. They describe psychology's return to memory research in the mid-1970s, with Robert Buckhout and Elizabeth Loftus, whose work drew wide attention. DNA exonerations then pushed the issue into public view.

segments.title: The Innocence Project and exoneration statistics
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Innocence Project's work overturning convictions based on faulty evidence. They cite about 365 exonerations and say many death-row convictions were based on eyewitness testimony, including cases with multiple witnesses.

segments.title: How perception fills in gaps
segments.summary: The hosts explain that people perceive reality piecemeal and fill in blanks, citing theories of perception and gestalt theory. They use the hollow-mask illusion as an example and note that the brain prioritizes threats in dangerous situations.

segments.title: Vision, eyesight and courtroom challenges
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how defense attorneys challenge witnesses on eyesight, lighting, distance and glasses. They mention Jeffrey Loftus's vision-over-distance formula and the Perry Mason courtroom jokes.

segments.title: Attention limits, attentional blink, and weapon focus
segments.summary: The hosts explain attentional blink and the psychological refractory period, which can cause witnesses to miss details during stressful events. They describe weapon focus, where attention goes to a gun rather than the face, and a personal story of a mugging victim who did not notice the gun.

segments.title: Cross-race effect and the Ronald Cotton case
segments.summary: The hosts explain the own-race bias or cross-race effect, which affects people regardless of prejudice scores. They describe the Ronald Cotton case, in which Jennifer Thompson misidentified him and Bobby Poole was the real perpetrator. DNA later exonerated Cotton, and Thompson and Cotton co-wrote the book Picking Cotton.

segments.title: Repeated recall, leading questions and confidence
segments.summary: The hosts explain how repeated retelling, leading questions and the misinformation effect change memory and build confidence over time. They note juries are swayed by confident witnesses, and that courts have often excluded expert testimony on memory as common sense. They describe the 1977 Supreme Court ruling with its five factors and the debate over whether confidence reflects accuracy.

segments.title: Troy Davis and wrongful execution
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 2011 execution of Troy Davis in Georgia for the killing of police officer Mark McPhail. They say nine eyewitnesses, seven of whom recanted, were the main evidence, and that a petition with about 660,000 signatures did not stop the execution.
